To be achieved on the 18th… will pass a distance of 25.9 billion㎞ from Earth

The farthest any artificial object has ever ventured into space

A ‘Golden Record’ for extraterrestrials is attached to the spacecraft

Includes the location of Earth within the Solar System, plus music and photographs

First stellar visit in 40,000 years… a step that broadens humanity

An artist rendering of Voyager 1 flying beyond the Solar System. On the 18th, it is expected to become the first human-made object to reach ‘one light-day’. Courtesy of NASA

Voyager 1 undergoes final checks in the assembly building at Kennedy Space Center in Florida about a week before its August 1977 launch. Courtesy of NASA

The long-range unmanned space probe Voyager 1, launched by NASA in 1977, will set a major record next week. Its distance from Earth will reach ‘one light-day’. Even traveling at the fastest speed in the universe, the speed of light (300,000㎞ per second), it would still take a full day to reach Voyager 1. No artificial object has ever advanced this far into space before.

Attached to the Voyager 1 spacecraft is a ‘self-introduction’ meant to tell extraterrestrial intelligent beings who humanity is. Some foresee that breaking the one-light-day barrier will be an opportunity to expand the scope of human thought further into the distant cosmos.

‘One light-day’ after 49 years since launch

According to NASA and the local scientific community last week, Voyager 1 will pass a point in space where its distance from Earth is one light-day, that is, 25.9 billion㎞, at 5:16:07 a.m. on the 18th (7:16:07 p.m. on the 18th, Korean time).

A light-day is the distance that light, traveling at 300,000㎞ per second, covers in exactly 24 hours. No human-made object has ever been this far from Earth. The distance between Earth and the Sun (150 million㎞) is reached in 8 minutes 20 seconds at light speed. Compared with one light-day, that is right next door.

About the size of a van and with a mass of 720㎏, Voyager 1 was launched by NASA on September 5, 1977 (local time). In human terms, its fiftieth birthday is in sight. Its current velocity is 60,000㎞ per hour, about 70 times the speed of an international airliner.

NASA said, “Even after Voyager 1 passes the point corresponding to one light-day, neither the surrounding environment nor the conditions inside the probe will change”. In other words, the routine of Voyager 1, flying through the quiet, dark expanse and even seeming monotonous, will continue.

Even so, reaching one light-day is clearly meaningful. Voyager 1 differs from ordinary space probes in its operational purpose. Along with space observation, it was built with the possibility of an accidental encounter with extraterrestrial intelligent life beyond the Solar System in mind. It was designed with the idea that beings beyond Earth who see Voyager 1 passing near their planet might decide to capture it out of curiosity. For such a scenario to occur, Voyager 1 must first travel far into deep space. This one-light-day milestone provides that springboard.

The ‘Golden Record’ attached to the Voyager 1 spacecraft. It is filled mainly with symbols that describe how to play back the stored recordings, and it also marks the location of Earth (the straight lines at lower left). Courtesy of NASA

Images included on the ‘Golden Record’. They depict everyday scenes of humanity. Courtesy of NASA

Introducing ‘humanity’ with the Golden Record

The equipment on Voyager 1 conceived with a meeting with extraterrestrial intelligent life in mind is the ‘Golden Record’. It is a self-introduction created by humanity. It is attached on the outside of Voyager 1 where it is easy to notice. The disc is copper plated with gold, and its diameter is 30㎝.

The Golden Record contains audio and visual materials to represent humans: 27 tracks of classical, popular, and folk music; 115 photographs, including scenes such as shopping in a market or rowing a boat; and greetings from 55 countries. Among the greetings is the Korean phrase “Hello?”. Engraved on the surface of the Golden Record are methods for building a device to play back the stored records and information such as the location of Earth.

The Golden Record was created under the leadership of Dr. Carl Sagan, a prominent American astronomer and advocate of science popularization. He is also the author of the science bestsellers <Cosmos> and <Pale Blue Dot>.

He thought that somewhere in this vast universe there would exist extraterrestrial life with civilizations similar to or more advanced than those of humanity. NASA said, “(Reaching one light-day) will prove the immensity of the universe and the remarkable durability of Voyager 1”.

First star in 40,000 years

Even so, given the scale of the universe, it is also worth viewing the one-light-day milestone with composure. In astronomy, the distance between stars is usually expressed not in light-days but in light-years. One light-year is the distance light travels in one year, amounting to 9.46 trillion㎞. Compared with a light-year, a light-day (25.9 billion㎞) is negligible. Many celestial bodies studied by astronomers are hundreds of millions of light-years away or more. In short, Voyager 1 still has a long way to go to serve fully as a messenger for humanity.

Given its current trajectory, Voyager 1's first arrival at an extraterrestrial star system will be in 40,000 years. It is expected to pass near Gliese 445, 17 light-years from Earth. No planets have been discovered near Gliese 445. Without planets, the likelihood of life is high to be low. It therefore appears that much more time will be needed before ‘contact’ between Voyager 1 and extraterrestrial life.

The space-observation instruments carried by Voyager 1 are expected to shut down in the early to mid-2030s due to insufficient power. Even so, Voyager 1's role as a messenger for humanity will continue. The Golden Record does not require electricity to remain attached or to preserve its contents.

Voyager 2, which shares a twin-structured spacecraft but follows a different trajectory, is expected in 2035 to become the second in history to reach one light-day.
